An El Niño climate pattern typically brings dangerous heat domes and hurricanes to the Pacific but experts have added to the list of threats this year: sea snakes and sharks.
White sharks - known commonly as great whites - are swimming off the California coast in greater numbers this year thanks to hotter ocean temperatures linked to this year’s supercharged El Niño.
"We expect to see all kinds of weird tropical things come up with this warm water," Douglas McCauley, director of the Benioff Ocean Initiative at the University of California, Santa Barbara, told USA Today.





One of those weird things is the venomous and tropical yellow-bellied sea snake.
A bite from this sea snake can lead to paralysis and death in just hours without treatment, according to the Australian Museum.

El Niño - the warm phase of a global climate pattern - has been tied to shifting populations of sea lions, turtles and fish in the past, too. There were Hammerhead shark bites reported off the Southern California coast during the 2015-2016 El Niño event, according to KNBC.
"We saw this fin and then it dove," kayaker Kyle Hudgins told the station after his friend Dylan Marks was bitten while kayaking near Santa Monica.

Andy Burnham’s new Energy Secretary has previously backed calls for frequent flyers to be charged a green tax on plane tickets. 
Miatta Fahnbulleh was chief executive of the New Economics Foundation (NEF) think-tank between 2017 and 2023, which advocated for a levy to help limit carbon emissions from flights. 
A report published in 2021 backed charges potentially worth hundreds of pounds to target people who fly regularly, replacing the current Air Passenger Duty (APD) system.

 
In the same year, the now Energy Secretary told The Independent that the Conservative government – which had announced a cut to APD on domestic flights – should be “raising, not cutting, taxes with a frequent flyer levy”. 
The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) has insisted that a frequent flyer levy is “not government policy,” and there is no suggestion Fahnbulleh will push for it as a minister – or that the Government is considering introducing one. 
But Fahnbulleh’s past support offers insight into her views on the environment and into the case made by campaigners and the Government’s own advisers for cutting emissions from frequent flying. 
What is a frequent flyer levy? 
Currently, the Government charges Air Passenger Duty (APD) on every passenger aged over 16 who departs from a UK airport. The aircraft operator pays the fee, but the cost is usually passed on to passengers through their ticket price.



 
The exact charge depends on the cabin class, type of aircraft and destination, and ranges from £8 for a domestic economy flight to £1,141 for a long-haul trip on a private jet. 
In 2021, the NEF and Possible climate charity proposed scrapping APD and replacing it with a new frequent flyer levy. 
Under the proposal, a passenger’s first leisure flight of the year would be tax-free, with each subsequent flight charged progressively more. Business flights would be taxed from the first trip. 
The idea, in short, is that a small number of wealthier, frequent flyers are responsible for a disproportionate share of flying-related emissions, so should pay more. In contrast, people who fly only once a year should pay less than they do now. 
The Government’s own climate advisers, the Climate Change Committee (CCC), also proposed a similar system in 2019. 
However, their preferred model works differently. Rather than a flat rate that rises purely with the number of flights taken, it would charge per tonne of carbon emitted, meaning the cost also depends on the distance flown and the class of ticket bought. 
As with NEF’s proposal, the first flight of the year would be exempt under this model too.

articles.title: Heat pumps can make your home ‘easier to sell’ – but won’t always add value
articles.raw_rss: A heat pump may not add its full installation cost to your property’s price, but experts say it could make an energy-efficient home more attractive to buyers
articles.raw_meta: A heat pump may not add its full installation cost to your property’s price, but experts say it could make an energy-efficient home more attractive to buyers
articles.jina_text:
As homeowners look for ways to cut their energy use and reduce their reliance on gas, increasingly, heat pumps are becoming an attractive alternative to gas boilers. They produce fewer carbon emissions and, in the right property, can help to lower heating costs. Government support has made the upfront investment more manageable, too, with eligible households able to claim up to £7,500 towards installation, through the Boiler Upgrade Scheme.
But a heat pump is still a major home improvement, and the financial calculation goes beyond running costs alone. Homeowners may also wonder whether installing one will make their property more appealing to future buyers, improve its energy performance certificate (EPC) rating or even increase its eventual sale price.
The answer is not straightforward. A well-designed system in an efficiently insulated home could become a valuable selling point, but experts caution that buyers rarely pay a pound-for-pound premium for energy upgrades. Here, surveyors, property specialists and housing experts explain what homeowners should consider before investing.

How heat pumps work
Heat pumps work by extracting heat from the air or ground outside and using it to provide heating and hot water within a property. Unlike conventional boilers, which cycle on and off as temperatures rise and fall, heat pumps operate more steadily, maintaining a consistent indoor temperature. 





Although electricity costs more than gas per unit, a heat pump can typically generate around three units of heat for every unit of electricity it consumes. This means energy bills can be lower, particularly when combined with off-peak electricity tariffs or solar panels.
Heat pumps can cost between £8,000 and £15,000 to install but upfront installation costs have become more manageable, thanks to the government's Boiler Upgrade Scheme, which offers homeowners up to £7,500 in grants. The average price to replace a gas boiler is around £2,000 to £3,000. With incentives in place, many homeowners are now asking whether a heat pump is also a genuine investment when it’s time to sell their property.

A shift in greener thinking
Paul Broadhead, head of mortgage and housing policy at the Building Societies Association, believes attitudes towards greener homes have changed significantly.


"What the volatility in energy prices has really focused people on is how much a property is going to cost to run. If you go back 15 or 20 years, the only focus for buyers was how much the property was going to cost to buy."

articles.jina_text:
A man inspects damage to his property in an area scorched by a wildfire near Vila Vella, Spain. Photograph: Damian Torres/AP
View image in fullscreen
A man inspects damage to his property in an area scorched by a wildfire near Vila Vella, Spain. Photograph: Damian Torres/AP


ECB official warns climate crisis poses growing threat to ‘core financial stability’


Exclusive: As wildfires rage, Frank Elderson says more work needed to assess risk from collapse of ecosystem services




A senior policymaker at the European Central Bank has said the climate emergency and the breakdown of nature poses a dramatically growing risk to the global economy.
Frank Elderson, a member of the ECB’s executive board, said the eurozone lender of last resort was stepping up its monitoring of the financial risks linked to the destruction of “ecosystem services”, which are nature-related processes or assets that support human activity.

“These services are not stable but they are in rapid decline. That’s why we talk about the climate and nature crises,” he said. “So knowing that dependency, and knowing those exposures by the banks, we come to the conclusion that this is relevant.”
Across France and Spain, wildfires have raged amid record-breaking temperatures, torching land, businesses and homes, in an emergency that will carry a heavy economic cost beside the direct human toll.



In an interview with the Guardian before the current devastation across Europe, Elderson said it was clear the rising frequency of natural disasters linked to global heating pos a threat to financial stability.
He said more work needed to be done to assess the risk from the collapse of ecosystem services, as reliance on nature was more complicated to map than the impact of a single extreme weather event.
Ecosystem services are defined as any benefit that can be drawn from a natural structure or process – for example, water can be used as a raw material, an energy source through hydropower, or for transportation. It is also a habitat for marine life critical for food production, and a basis for recreational services.
“Nature-related risks can pose material economic and financial risks, including through their impacts on credit risk, growth, inflation and – over the long-term – potential financial instability,” Elderson said.
“I did interviews [previously] saying, you know, if you destroy nature, you destroy the core on which our economies depend. And that got people’s attention. This is not some kind of a flower-power, tree-hugging exercise. This is core economics. This is core financial stability, core price stability.”


As the supervisor responsible for Europe’s largest banks, the ECB has launched a programme of work to assess how the escalating damage to ecosystem services could expose the financial system to risk.
The central bank plans to publish analysis later this year investigating how “ecosystem degradation pathways” could translate into credit loss dynamics for the eurozone’s banks.

articles.raw_meta: António Guterres says strengthening El Niño will help push the world’s climate crisis into ‘uncharted territory’
articles.jina_text:
India’s monsoon is in danger and hotter, drier conditions are forecast across much of the world as a stronger El Niño weather system is taking hold, weather experts have warned.
António Guterres, the UN secretary general, said the strengthening El Niño was “adding fuel to a planet already on fire” and pushing the world into “uncharted territory”.

The El Niño system will strengthen from August to October, which will bring higher temperatures globally, with increasing rainfall in some regions while others suffer drought, according to data and forecasts released by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) on Friday.
Marine heatwaves have already shocked scientists this year and are set to intensify: the WMO said temperatures were likely to exceed 2.9C above normal in several regions.



“The Pacific waters driving it have never been this warm this early in an El Niño, and temperatures are still increasing,” Guterres said. “[This year] risks shattering every seasonal record, and driving even more severe effects worldwide. We are in uncharted territory.”
The risk of a weakened monsoon, which brings the rain on which Indian farmers rely, was highlighted as the forecast gave an “enhancement in the probability for below-normal rainfall”, which would produce increased drought, floods and wildfire risk around the Indian Ocean basin. Drier conditions are also likely across parts of equatorial Africa to the west of the Horn of Africa, across the south and east of Australia, large parts of South America and in North America.
Higher than normal rainfall is expected in southern Europe, central Asia and the Horn of Africa and south-eastern South America.
Extreme weather has already caused havoc around the world this summer, with record-breaking heatwaves beginning in May in the UK, and wildfires across France and Spain that have destroyed villages and displaced hundreds of thousands of people.


View image in fullscreen
A destroyed house after wildfires in the village of Le Porge, Gironde, France. Photograph: Catalina Martin-Chico/The Guardian


Scientists have warned this year of the development of an El Niño, a weather system in the Pacific that frequently affects temperatures and rainfall around the world. Some El Niño years in the past have been relatively mild, but scientists have said that this year’s has been supercharged by the climate crisis.
Warmer waters – earlier in the year than usual and with water temperatures still increasing – have led to predictions of a “super El Niño” forming. The WMO does not use this term, but has said that the weather system developing is likely to be significantly stronger and more intense than usual. Friday’s forecasts were the organisation’s latest update, covering August to October.

articles.title: Council cancels climate emergency declaration
articles.raw_rss: A Reform UK motion argues the council can improve the local environment without the official pledge.
articles.raw_meta: A Reform UK motion argues the council can improve the local environment without the official pledge.
articles.jina_text:
A local authority has voted to scrap a borough's climate emergency declaration, despite opposition from rival councillors and environmental campaigners.
South Tyneside's Reform UK councillors backed a motion at Thursday's full council meeting to rescind the 2019 pledge, arguing the authority could continue improving the local environment without maintaining the declaration.
The motion, brought by cabinet member for housing Steve Smith, said: "Core services, economic growth and the cost of living should take priority over climate targets that are not statutory requirements."
The motion was passed by 35 votes to 11.
Opposition councillors warned the move would weaken the Reform-led council's response to climate change and whether it would deliver any financial benefit, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.
The original motion, launched by the Green Party, set out deadlines for the council to become carbon neutral, aligning strategic decisions, policies and strategies to this goal, as well as advocating for carbon reduction across the borough.
'False choice'
Smith's motion asked the council to "rescind" the pledge and request council officers to "review any policies, targets and spending commitments" introduced as a result of the declaration.





Advertisement












It also asked the council to "reaffirm its commitment to clean streets, parks, recycling, flood protection and other local environmental services that matter to residents" and to ensure future environmental initiatives are only pursued where they are "affordable, evidence-based and delivering clear benefits" for residents.
But councillor Rachael Taylor, Green group leader, said the motion "created a false choice between climate action and delivering good local services".
She said the council already "considers affordability, value for money and evidence before spending public money" and there was no evidence rescinding the declaration would save money or improve services.
Meanwhile councillor Kate Owens-Palmer, of the South Tyneside Alliance Group, said she was "perplexed" that the motion stated Reform wanted to rescind the climate emergency declaration, while at the same time, pledging to "do all the things that are going to protect nature and look after the climate".
The council meeting followed a demonstration from environmental campaigners outside South Shields Town Hall raising concerns about the motion.

Tim Young on Grange Farm in Hockwold, Norfolk. His onion crop is 35% down in yield on last year because of the heat and drought. Photograph: Jason Bye/The Guardian


‘It’s too fast, too big’: speed of climate crisis is devastating crops, say farmers


Drought and extreme heat are killing plants, driving up prices while also making some farms economically unviable




“It’s a constant battle,” says Tim Young. He and his family have been tracking the rainfall on their Norfolk farm since 1976, and the data shows the last six years have seen two-thirds the amount of rain compared with previous years. The lack of water has become the number one risk to Young’s business.
This summer has seen record-breaking climate induced heatwaves scorch much of Europe, which combined with droughts and “apocalyptic” wildfires has made farming virtually impossible. France has faced down fires that its president, Emmanuel Macron, called the worst since the second world war and on Wednesday half of England was declared officially in drought, with July expected to be the driest on record after winter floods, according to the Environment Agency. So how are farmers bearing up under the pressure?



“The vines are dying. The grass is yellow and now we can smell the smoke,” Uyen Do, an organic farmer in the Dordogne region of France says, almost in tears. “It’s already very difficult to survive economically and now with climate change it’s becoming a struggle that I’m not sure we’re capable of going through.”
Do took over the farm in 2018 and adopted organic farming practices in the hope to build resilience against the climate crisis. But with the climate changing much faster than most predicted, Do says her farm is just not able to adapt quickly enough. “It’s too fast. It’s too big,” she says.


View image in fullscreen
The grain store on Tim Young’s farm in Hockwold, Norfolk is holding far less than usual this year because of the drought. Photograph: Jason Bye/The Guardian


Young has struggled too, despite a much longer career in farming. Last year, the Environment Agency paused his licence to take water from the nearby river owing to low river flows, which he says had catastrophic impacts on his farm. He keeps anxiously checking his phone to see what the latest update will bring.
“In July, we had just 0.2mm of rain,” he says. “We’re so reliant upon that message.”
He would like to build a reservoir on his farm to store water in periods of intense rainfall and high river flows, but says cost and planning permission has always been a key barrier. He recently had to buy water from another farmer at an inflated price and so building a reservoir increasingly seems like an essential business decision.

articles.title: Wildfire on Suffolk coast near nuclear power station ‘stabilised’
articles.raw_rss: The fire is a few miles away from Sizewell B and the construction site for the new Sizewell C.
articles.raw_meta: The fire is a few miles away from Sizewell B and the construction site for the new Sizewell C.
articles.jina_text:
Fire crews battling a large wildfire near Britain’s biggest nuclear power station said the blaze has stabilised overnight, but have warned that the risk of fresh outbreaks remains high.




The fire near Sizewell B on the Suffolk coast has devastated an area equivalent to around 210 football pitches and forced locals and holidaymakers to flee.








Deputy chief fire officer for Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service Henry Griffin told reporters on Friday that an investigation has been launched into how the fire started at RSPB Minsmere and then spread to nearby heathland.




His firefighters have been tackling the blaze in Dunwich Heath, near Leiston, since Wednesday evening, with more than 100 firefighters deployed and a helicopter being used to drop thousands of litres of seawater onto the burning land.




The fire is a few miles away from Sizewell B and the construction site for the new Sizewell C, though authorities stressed there was no concern about the fire spreading towards the power station.


The blaze caused holidaymakers to flee (Joe Giddens/PA)
PA Wire




Mr Griffin said: “We have a couple of fire fronts we are actively monitoring, checking on their wind speed, checking on that wind direction, to make sure any reignition is controlled and monitored throughout the coming hours.











“Due to the scale and unpredictable nature of the wind direction I wouldn’t say it is under control, it’s certainly stabilised and we have plans in place to mitigate.”




Mr Griffin said he wanted to offer “thanks and praise” to every firefighter working on tackling the fire, saying their welfare was of “primary importance”.







He added: “That’s something we’re actively looking at now so that we can get people back to their belongings, back to their vehicles, to get away from their holiday locations, because the risk will remain high over the coming days of fire reignition.”


The blaze is close to Britain’s biggest nuclear power station (Joe Giddens/PA)
PA Wire




On Thursday, the service said the area affected had grown to 150 hectares with 18 fire engines and more than 100 firefighters at the scene.

articles.jina_text:
The UK may see some relief from the back-to-back heatwaves over the weekend as forecasters say temperatures are set to be cooler with a chance of light rain.
Many experienced the country’s fourth heatwave of the year in July, with temperatures reaching 35.2C on Wednesday – the seventh day in 2026 when temperatures have hit 35C or higher.
Paired with severely low rainfall, the hot weather has led to official drought conditions being declared for regions home to around half of England’s population, and the entirety of Wales.





Several other areas remain in high-risk prolonged dry weather status, with only north-east England and Scotland retaining normal status.

Parts of the North will be “chilly” on Friday, with light showers, the Met Office has said. It added: “Temperatures are expected to be much closer to average across most of the UK, and even slightly below average for northern Scotland.”

But southern regions are not set to see much rainfall, with weather forecast to remain largely dry.

“However, it looks as though amounts of rain for many will be fairly modest, and won't balance out the shortfall that we have recorded this summer. It’s still possible that some areas of the South will miss out and see little or no rainfall.”
The continued dry weather has prompted a string of wildfires across the UK, with fire chiefs warning that they are becoming a “recurring and growing feature of the risks facing our communities”.



July has seen firefighters tackle a record number of wildfires, at 393 in England and Wales. The number of wildfires in 2026 is now higher than the combined total of 2021, 2023, and 2024, but remains below the same point in 2025 when drought conditions were also experienced.

New solar panels in Great Britain at 15-year high as fossil fuel costs soar


Boom in solar farms and home installations in first half of 2026 began shortly after start of US-Israel war against Iran




Great Britain has recorded more new solar power installations in the first half of this year than in any six-month period since 2011, as households turn to rooftop panels to help cut their energy bills.
An analysis of the government’s official figures shows that Great Britain added 142,536 solar installations in the first six months of the year, putting it on track to top last year’s record solar additions.

The government data, which includes large ground-mounted solar farms and rooftop panels, showed that the half-year solar boom is second only to the record 167,316 installations recorded in the second half of 2011, when the first large-scale solar farm was built in Cornwall on the site of a disused tin mine.
Most of the new solar installations recorded in the government’s official figures are on household rooftops, although these smaller solar systems make up slightly less than a third of the country’s total solar power capacity.

More households have fitted solar panels to their rooftops in recent years, hoping to cut their energy bills by generating their own low-cost electricity as fossil fuels have caused bills to rocket, according to energy companies.
The government’s data shows that more households are taking up grants to replace their gas boilers with low-carbon heating alternatives. The total number of applications for the boiler upgrade scheme reached 4,512 last month, up by 21% compared with June last year.
Heat pumps are expected to be in higher demand in the months ahead after the government raised its grant funding by 20% last week, from £7,500 to £9,000, to help cover the costs of replacing fossil fuel heating. Andy Burnham has also cut VAT on electricity bills from October, which makes running a heat pump cheaper.


E.ON Next, which is expected to become the UK’s biggest energy retailer, said it has recorded a 151% rise in the number of homes installing solar panels in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year.

Suffolk wildfire near Sizewell nuclear plant ‘stabilising’ after 24 hours


More than 100 firefighters remain at scene after Dunwich Heath blaze spread across 150 hectares and forced evacuations




Fire crews tackling a large wildfire burning for more than 24 hours near Britain’s biggest nuclear power station have said the situation is “stabilising”.
More than 100 firefighters have been battling the blaze in Dunwich Heath, near Leiston, on the Suffolk coast since Wednesday evening.

By late Thursday, while the incident remained “dynamic”, Suffolk fire and rescue service said the blaze appeared to be stablising.
At least 12 fire appliances remained at the scene overnight to tackle smaller fires breaking out, while crews monitored identified hotspots.
A fire service spokesperson said: “Although the fire is dynamic, it remains stable and Suffolk fire and rescue service is making good progress.”

Firefighting efforts have included a helicopter capable of dropping 100 litres of seawater on each pass and six London fire brigade appliances.


Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Friday morning, the deputy chief fire officer for Suffolk fire and rescue service, Henry Griffin, said an investigation had been launched into the cause of the fire and that the blaze had “stabilised”.
He added: “We have a couple of fire fronts we are actively monitoring, checking on their wind speed, checking on that wind direction, to make sure any reignition is controlled and monitored throughout the coming hours.
“Due to the scale and unpredictable nature of the wind direction … I would not use the words to say it is ‘under control’, but I am confident we have the resources in place and a plan in place to mitigate any risks of this fire.”


View image in fullscreen
A firefighter tackles flames on Dunwich Heath. Photograph: Suffolk fire and rescue service


The “unprecedented” wildfire, which broke out at about 5pm on Wednesday, grew approximately 150 hectares, about 370 acres or the equivalent of 210 football pitches.
The blaze is a few miles from Sizewell B nuclear power station and the construction site for the new Sizewell C plant.
Freddie Gulliver, an emergency manager at the Suffolk Joint Emergency Planning Unit, said there was no immediate concern about the fire spreading towards Sizewell B.
A spokesperson for the energy supplier EDF said the wildfire was “not affecting operations” at Sizewell B, adding that the company was closely monitoring the situation. The spokesperson said the site had emergency plans covering a range of scenarios, including a fire on the premises.

articles.jina_text:
Emergency services in the Gironde department of France work to contain wildfires this week. Photograph: Mael Dubiez/SDIS33/EPA
View image in fullscreen
Emergency services in the Gironde department of France work to contain wildfires this week. Photograph: Mael Dubiez/SDIS33/EPA


‘Extremely scary findings’ show climate crisis is supercharging Europe’s wildfire weather


Latest study says global heating has made hot, dry and windy conditions in Spain at least 20 times more likely




The extreme heat and drought stoking huge wildfires in Spain and France were made far more likely by the climate crisis, a scientific analysis has found.
Global heating made hot, dry and windy weather at least 20 times more likely in Spain and twice as likely in France, experts from the World Weather Attribution (WWA) consortium calculated. The finding is the latest to pin the blame for the continent’s sweltering and deadly summer firmly on the heating caused by the burning of oil, gas and coal.

The intense heatwave at the end of June, which is estimated to have killed 20,000 people, could not have happened without the extra heat trapped by carbon pollution, a previous WWA study showed. Another found that the climate crisis-driven heat was “sucking soils dry” as extreme drought spread across Europe.


Searing heat and parched land led to very high “daily severity ratings”, the metric that was used in the new analysis and which measures how severe a wildfire will be if ignited. Studies of the 2025 wildfires also found they were supercharged by the climate crisis.
This year’s wildfires in western Europe have been made worse by a wet winter and spring, which boosted the growth of vegetation, which then dried out and provided fuel for the fires – so-called whiplash conditions. Global heating is making winters wetter and summers drier and hotter in Europe.

When Stefan Rahmstorf walked through the ruined streets of Dresden after the river Elbe flooded in 2002, and again when severe heat killed 70,000 people in Europe the following summer, the German climatologist wondered if worsening weather would make the political world “wake up and do something really decisively” to cut emissions.
But two decades and 750bn tons of atmospheric carbon pollution later, Rahmstorf is still wondering when the wake-up call will come. Last week, as he was surfing off France’s Atlantic coast with his partner, he watched towering smoke plumes darken the sky as a ferocious inferno raged outside Bordeaux.

“The sun through the smoke was looking really blood red, and it put the whole landscape into an eerie orange-coloured tint, like being on Mars or in some dystopian sci-fi movie,” says Rahmstorf. “It felt totally surreal.”


Europe is suffering through a hellish summer of relentless heat. I’m writing this from Berlin, where temperatures are set to reach 37C (99F) on Thursday – and ferocious wildfires that have broken records in France and Spain.
What are the impacts of this, and should it really have come as a surprise? All that and more, after the headlines.
Essential reads

Yet as he looked back to the land from his surfboard on Wednesday last week, he saw a plume of smoke rising behind the dunes. Two days later, the fire that had caused it it had escalated into a blaze so great it generated a rare thunderstorm cloud capable of igniting even more fires. Rahmstorf cut his holiday in Lacanau a day short and headed to smoke-choked Bordeaux on Friday evening, eager to take the train back to Germany the next day.
“The air was much better when we woke up Saturday morning,” he says. “But the idea of having to inhale this kind of air for any length of time seemed something we really wanted to avoid.”
This summer’s fire weather across the EU has broken records for severity for this time of year, data published on Thursday shows, while more of France has already burned than in any previous full year on record. More than 300,000 people across France and Spain were forced to flee homes and tourist accommodation within a week, and some are returning to burned-out homes and destroyed belongings.

articles.title: Satellite images show impact of heatwaves and drought on UK landscape
articles.raw_rss: BBC Verify's analysis indicates “vegetation stress” in many areas, which may affect wildlife and farming.
articles.raw_meta: BBC Verify's analysis indicates “vegetation stress” in many areas, which may affect wildlife and farming.
articles.jina_text:
We can see parts of the country are suffering from "vegetation stress" where the development and growth of plants, grass and crops can be severely affected.
Experts have said the combination of next-to-no rainfall and prolonged hot weather is likely to cause significant issues for the farming industry and have an impact on agriculture and food supplies.
Scientists also warn the UK is facing a growing risk of water shortages in the decades ahead, driven by human-caused climate change and increased demand.









A comparison of satellite imagery of the UK in May and July shows the stark differences in plant health. To assess this, we have used something called the Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) - a measure of how green and healthy vegetation is.
The biggest changes are visible across Conwy, Flintshire, Denbighshire and Merseyside, where areas that were previously a patchwork of green fields and grassland are now covered by light brown tones, indicating extensive vegetation stress.









Elsewhere, the data highlights more localised hotspots of stress around Peterborough, Lincolnshire and parts of mid and east Devon, where fields also appear significantly browner than a year ago.









This is in stark contrast to upland Britain - including much of Scotland's highlands and the Welsh mountains - which has remained closer to normal or, in some places, appear slightly greener.
Vegetation turning brown, even on this scale, does not mean the plants have disappeared or died, as grass, shrubs and some trees can recover once rainfall returns, provided their root systems remain intact.
However, falling groundwater levels during prolonged dry periods can also remove an important backup water source for trees and other deep-rooted vegetation.
And perhaps counter-intuitively, prolonged dry weather can raise the risk of flash flooding when it eventually does rain. That is because parched, rock-hard ground may struggle to absorb water at first, so some rainwater may simply run off the surface instead.









Dr Jess Neumann, an associate professor at the University of Reading, said while it is not unusual to see some browning in the summer, the "large expanses of dry grass in parks, lawns and gardens" are particularly noticeable this year.
Neumann added that British plants are "not adapted to prolonged summer droughts and hot weather", unlike in places like the Mediterranean.
This summer's "flash" drought is also notable for how quickly it has developed, given in early spring river flows, soil moisture and reservoir levels were generally around or above normal following a very wet start to 2026.
The recent repeated heatwaves have sapped moisture from soils and vegetation via evaporation, which has in turn increased demand for water for farming, industry and household use.
"The drought could have a direct knock-on effect on food supplies," said Dr Pauline Scheelbeek, associate professor at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicin

articles.jina_text:
Climate change made the extreme conditions behind the wildfires burning across France and Spain far more likely, new analysis has found.
The study, released by the World Weather Attribution group on Friday, found that human-caused warming made the hot, dry and windy conditions that fuelled the fires at least twice as likely in south-western France and at least 20 times as likely in central Spain. The scientists described both figures as conservative estimates.
Fires have burned across the two countries since early July, destroying thousands of homes and displacing more than 250,000. They have been described as some of the worst on record in both countries, with 140,000 hectares burned in Spain and 115,000 in France since the start of the year, an area larger than the Isle of Wight in each case. 





Some blazes grew so fierce they generated their own weather systems, making them very hard to contain, and further high temperatures are forecast in both countries in the coming days.
Researchers examined the seven-day period of most dangerous fire weather in the worst-hit areas, using a measure called the Daily Severity Rating, which combines heat, dryness, wind and landscape conditions to gauge how hard a fire would be to put out once it started. They compared this year's conditions with observations of past summers and with a simulated pre-industrial climate.

articles.jina_text:
Scores of firefighters battled more large grass fires in east London on Thursday amid the ongoing threat of severe wildfires in the capital.




Dramatic pictures showed a blaze ripping across grassland in Hornchurch. A fire also destroyed a large area of land in Rainham.


Parkland in Hornchurch ablaze due to the dry conditions
PA




The cause of both fires in the borough of Havering is under investigation.




It comes after around 120 firefighters battled two major grass fires in Romford, east London, on Wednesday.




The risk from blazes in capital, now officially in a drought, is “very high” currently, according to a Natural England fire severity index.








London Fire Brigade (LFB) had its busiest 24 hours of 2026 on Wednesday, tackling 63 grass fires across the capital as temperatures topped 30C (86F).




Control officers took more than 1,300 emergency calls and crews went to more than 500 incidents, the brigade said. 




Almost 1,000 calls about grass fires have been made in the past week.




Eight fire engines and around 60 firefighters tackled the grass fire near South End Road in Hornchurch on Thursday.




At the height of the fire, around six hectares was alight, the London Fire Brigade said. 




The LFB was first called to the fire at 1.18pm with the fire brought under control by 3.22pm. 


Parkland in Hornchurch ablaze due to the dry conditions
PA




Soon after eight fire engines and around 60 firefighters were called to another grass fire near Berwick Pond Road in nearby Rainham. 













The Brigade's Control Officers took the first of 11 calls at 3.35pm and the fire was under control by 5.12pm.




To battle both blazes, firefighters used backpack blowers, which work just like leaf blowers.




They allow firefighters to push flames back into already burnt areas.




This is a tactic that provides a faster, more efficient attack on wildfires.




Wildfire beaters were also being used. The beater is made of a long handle with a flat piece of rubber at the end.


Firefighters spray water over the burnt ground at the site of a wildfire in Hornchurch,
AFP/Getty




They’re used to beat the flames, which deprives them of oxygen and cools them down.




 Assistant commissioner Andy Pennick said the past 24 hours had been "incredibly challenging" for firefighters and control staff, who had faced “arduous, hot conditions”.









“In these hot, dry conditions, grass fires can spread incredibly quickly, threatening homes, wildlife and the environment, while tying up vital emergency resources,” he said.




Mr Pennick urged people not to use disposable barbecues in parks or open spaces, to dispose of cigarettes responsibly and to take litter home if bins were full.

articles.jina_text:
London has been baking in its fourth heatwave of the summer in recent days and has been experiencing its longest dry spell in years.




The capital is among areas of England suffering from “flash drought” as a result of very low rainfall and high temperatures and is also under a hosepipe ban from Thames Water.








With the exception of a small flurry of showers on July 5, the capital hasn’t seen a proper downpour in over a month, stretching back to June 27.




So when a small amount of rain fell on Thursday evening in parts of the capital, people took to social media to celebrate, albeit with a touch of irony over how little fell.
























According to the Met Office’s rain tracker map, the first rain fall began over the southwest of the capital at around 5.30pm before beginning to drift over the south of the capital.




However most saw very small amounts, with the majority seeing it falling at a rate of less than 0.5mm falling per hour. 




Although there were showers in some areas, including Croydon and Richmond.




There is the chance of further rainfall in the coming hours and the early hours of Friday, before weather is predicted to be dry again until the middle of next week when light rain showers are expected every day for most of the rest of the week.

articles.jina_text:
The whole of Wales is now in drought, as the UK struggles with extreme heat, wildfires and dry conditions that experts warn may linger until the autumn.




The UK has endured its fourth heatwave of the summer, with temperatures topping 35C, as health authorities warned England is on track this year for the highest number of deaths caused by such hot spells since current figures began.








Natural Resources Wales (NRW) has extended its drought declaration – which was declared for North Wales and the Upper Severn last week – to cover the whole of the country, after very little rainfall and sustained high temperatures.




Wales has received just 8% of its long-term average rainfall for July, and the country is on course to have its driest July since records began 190 years ago, NRW said.




Half of England is officially in drought, despite a very wet winter, as an extremely dry July compounded a dry spring, and the successive heatwaves have put pressure on water resources.




Fire chiefs say that wildfires are becoming a “recurring and growing feature of the risks facing our communities” in the face of a changing climate, as data showed July has been the busiest month on record, with firefighters responding to 393 wildfires across England and Wales.











The number of wildfire incidents recorded this year already matches the total annual figures seen in 2021, 2023, and 2024 combined, although the number is below the same point in 2025 when long-lasting drought and heat caused severe fire risk.




Phil Garrigan, chairman of the National Fire Chiefs Council, said: “Wildfires are no longer isolated or seasonal events. They are becoming a recurring and growing feature of the risks facing our communities and emergency services.”


(PA Graphics)
PA Graphics




He said blazes could burn for days in remote locations, challenging terrain and extreme temperatures, as he called for sustained investment in specialist training, modern equipment and research and technology to improve prevention and response.







Fire chiefs are also urging people to take simple actions such as disposing of cigarettes safely, avoiding the use of disposable barbecues and taking litter home, to significantly reduce the risk of fires starting.




In the latest wildfire, properties including a holiday park were evacuated and roads closed as firefighters battled a large heathland blaze on the Suffolk coast, at Dunwich Heath.

Ferocious flames continue to rage in parts of France and Spain, with no sign of abating. We chart the destruction in graphics and pictures

By Damian Carrington, Lucy Swan, Ana Lucía González Paz, Harvey Symons




The hellish infernos that have torn through parts of France and Spain have caused deaths, the evacuation of 330,000 people from their homes, widespread destruction and clouds of toxic smoke. Records have already been smashed and with the fourth heatwave of the European summer setting in, there are few signs of the waves of wildfires ending.
France has already surpassed the worst previous year for the size of the area burned, with August, usually the hottest month, yet to come.


In Spain, the cumulative number of fires in 2026 has also set a new record for this time of year, and the cumulative burnt area remains just below the level reached by late July during a devastating fire season in 2022.

Why have the wildfires been so bad?
The extreme severity of the blazes is the result of “whiplash” wet-then-dry weather this year, supercharged by the climate crisis. Last winter and much of spring in western Europe was very wet, encouraging heavy growth of trees, shrubs and other vegetation.



However, by May the first of a series of heatwaves had hit Europe. All heatwaves are made more intense and more likely by the global heating caused by fossil fuel burning. The heatwave at the end of June was the most severe ever recorded in Europe and would have been impossible without the added heat from more than a century of carbon pollution.
Western Europe’s hottest June

The high temperatures meant the hot atmosphere strongly evaporated water from rivers and lakes and sucked plants and soil dry, with the conditions made 80 times more likely by global heating. As a result of the drought conditions, vegetation became tinder and the risk of wildfires soared, leading to a series of wildfires scientists have described as “firewaves”.



The situation has been worsened by the unprecedented development of enormous “fire clouds” – pyrocumulonimbus – in France. These form from the heat from huge fires and become a self-feeding firestorm, spitting lightning bolts and sparking further blazes.


View image in fullscreen
A pyrocumulonimbus, or ‘fire cloud’, in the Fontainebleau forest region, about 37 miles south of Paris, France. Photograph: Emma Da Silva/AP


View image in fullscreen
Firefighters use controlled burning to halt a wildfire near Cebreros, Ávila province, Spain.  Photograph: Manu Fernández/AP
The severity of the fires has been extremely challenging for the fire-fighting authorities, who in the past would have expected to extinguish the fires. One firefighter, Javier García, told Associated Press he had never faced anything like it in his two decades in the job.


“The evolution is alarming,” he said, adding that they were now prioritising evacuations and property protection because fast-moving walls of flames were too ferocious.

articles.jina_text:
England is on track to record its highest ever number of heat-related deaths this summer after the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) announced that an estimated 2,877 people had died in the May and June heatwaves.
The record was set in 2022 with 2,985 deaths, and August, traditionally the hottest month, is yet to arrive. The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, said: “My thoughts are with all those who have lost loved ones as a result of the long and intense heatwaves.”

The UKHSA analysis estimated there were 753 deaths in the the heatwave from 24 to 27 May and a further 2,124 between 21 and 28 June. The total is almost double the figure for the whole summer in 2025.
The UKHSA estimate is based on recorded deaths. It calculates the excess mortality during the heatwaves when compared with mortality levels at similar times of the year that did not experience heatwaves. The figures are similar to an estimate published on 13 July that used a different method, based on data showing the link between heat and deaths in the past.



Heatwaves are made more intense and more likely by the fossil-fuel-driven climate crisis; the heatwave that affected western Europe at the end of June was the most severe and widespread ever. The heat in 2027 will be exacerbated by a looming super El Niño weather system and temperatures will continue to rise until carbon emissions are cut to net zero.
“The new figures highlight the significant danger that very hot weather can pose to people’s health,” said Dr Ross Thompson, principal environmental public health scientist at UKHSA. “As the climate becomes warmer, we can expect periods of hot weather to become longer, more frequent and more extreme. That’s why it’s vital that individuals, communities and systems are prepared to deal with higher temperatures, and to ensure those most vulnerable are protected.
Cooper said this summer’s heat was having “an increasingly serious impact on the health of thousands of people, and on the pressures facing our NHS too. My heartfelt thanks go to the NHS staff, care workers and emergency responders who have worked tirelessly through these exceptionally busy and challenging months to protect and care for people affected by the heat.”
Some ambulance services reported a record number of calls during the heatwaves.


During the June heatwave in England a new high temperature for the month, of 38C, was recorded at Lingwood, Norfolk, while the 31.5C recorded at Kew Gardens in May was a new record for that month.
Dr Garyfallos Konstantinoudis, of Imperial College London and co-author of the 13 July study, said: “The UKHSA’s analysis provides clear, tragic confirmation of the significant health impact these heatwaves had across England and Wales. Extended periods of extreme heat place immense strain on the human body.

articles.title: Suffolk wildfire latest: Firefighters battle blaze near huge nuclear power plant with major incident declared
articles.raw_rss: Fire crews are warning people to stay away from the area as residents are evacuated
articles.raw_meta: Fire crews are warning people to stay away from the area as residents are evacuated
articles.jina_text:
Firefighters are tackling a huge blaze near a nuclear power plant in Suffolk as authorities declared a “major incident” and residents have been evacuated.
At least 90 firefighters are tackling the “large-scale, wind- driven forestry fire” which broke out on Dunwich Heath shortly after 5:30pm on Wednesday, the Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service said.
Residents in several coastal properties and caravans have been evacuated as crews issued an urgent plea for people to stay away from the area.





There is no current risk to Sizewell B – a nuclear power station which provides electricity to 2.5 million households – due to the distance of the fire, but firefighters warn it is a “live and dynamic situation”.
It comes after forecasters warned any wildfires that break out in the South of England this week could become “exceptionally severe” due to a prolonged spell of hot and dry weather across the country.
The UK has experienced record-breaking temperatures this summer, with four heatwaves and a severe dry spell that has left the landscape parched.


At the height of the third heatwave in mid-July, firefighters were battling 19 significant wildfires simultaneously in England and Wales.
Have you been affected by the wildfire in Suffolk? We’d like to hear from you. Please email nicole.wootton-cane@independent.co.uk




15 minutes ago

Parts of the UK have been without rain for more than 40 days

Parts of the UK have been without rain for more than 40 days before a devastating wildfire broke out on Dunwich Heath.

Met Office data shows that at the start of the week, Wisley, in Surrey, had had 40 consecutive “dry days”, in which no or only a trace of rain has been recorded, while Herstmonceux, West End, in East Sussex had 37 dry days.

A number of other sites including Suffolk, where the fire has broken out, Heathrow in London and spots in Worcestershire, Norfolk, Cambridgeshire, Bedfordshire and Lincolnshire have all recorded more than 30 consecutive dry days.

Earlier this week a National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC) spokesperson warned: “With the Met Office warning that a fourth heatwave could develop this week, bringing another period of very hot weather to parts of the UK, fire and rescue services remain on alert and are continuing to prepare for renewed wildfire risk.”

London is facing the threat of severe wildfires as forecasts show little sign of rain in the capital. 




The risk from blazes in capital, now officially in a drought, is “very high” today according to a Natural England fire severity index.











It comes after around 120 firefighters battled two major grass fires in Romford, east London, yesterday.




In Suffolk, a major incident has been declared after a large heathland blaze erupted on the coast at Dunwich Heath, near Leiston.











Temperatures in London are expected to ease today with a high of 27C predicted after a high of 34C yesterday. 




Follow the latest updates below...


  
Live updates






  2 minutes ago

Number of heatwave-related deaths doubled compared to 2025




There have been almost double the number of excess deaths caused by heatwaves so far this year than in last summer, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has said.




A new report estimates there were 2,877 heat-associated deaths during the heatwaves in May and June this year, almost double the figure reported from the UK heatwaves in June to August last year.




An estimated 753 deaths were associated with the May heatwave from May 24-27, and a further 2,124 with the June heatwave between June 21 and 28.




“While these figures remain interim, they are already approaching the annual record reported by UKHSA in 2022,” the report said.




  15 minutes ago

Is the heatwave over?




Three consecutive days of temperatures exceeding 28C is required for it to be considered a heatwave. 




Today is set to peak at 27C, which could mark the end of London’s fourth heatwave. But, only time will tell whether this latest heatwave is truly over. 

The fourth heatwave of the year could be coming to an end

Parts of the capital are facing an “exceptionally high” wildfire threat as London sees one of its longest spells without a single drop of rain.

Major incident declared in Suffolk as 90 firefighters tackle wildfire on heathland


Several people evacuated after ‘large-scale, wind-driven’ fire breaks out at Dunwich Heath near Leiston




A major incident has been declared as firefighters battle a large heathland fire on the Suffolk coast.
Suffolk fire and rescue service was called to reports of a wildfire at Dunwich Heath, near Leiston, shortly after 5.30pm on Wednesday, and crews remained at the scene on Thursday morning. About 90 firefighters were tackling the blaze, while several people had been evacuated. Leiston is about 5km away from Sizewell B, but firefighters have said there is not thought to be any danger to the nuclear power station at this time.

The service said a major incident had been declared “due to the size and complexity” of the blaze. People have been urged to avoid the area where possible and keep windows and doors closed.


View image in fullscreen
Smoke rising from the fire. Photograph: Suffolk fire and rescue service
In an update on Thursday morning, the fire service said: “At this time there is no current risk to Sizewell B, due to the distance from the fire and the direction it is travelling (easterly). However, this is a live and dynamic situation and as a result any further updates will be shared accordingly.”


As a precaution, crews have been focused on protecting nearby properties, while preparations have been made for the potential to evacuate about 200 caravans at the Cliff House holiday park if conditions deteriorate.
Dan Davis, a station manager with Suffolk fire and rescue service, said: “Crews from Leiston attended the scene and were met with what is a large-scale, wind-driven forestry fire.
“The incident has subsequently been upgraded to a major incident. We currently have approximately 90 firefighters on scene working incredibly hard in arduous conditions to bring this fire under control.”
People displaced by the fire have been advised to attend Westleton Village Hall at 8am for further updates.
Specialist drones were being overnight to assess fire behaviour and support operational decision-making, while crews also deployed multipurpose all-wheel-drive Unimogs and 4x4 quad bikes.
The UK Health Security Agency had issued an amber heat-health alert for the East Midlands, the east and south-east of England and London, which was to remain in place until 9am on Thursday. The agency has warned that rising temperatures could increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups.
In Scotland, crews said they were making significant progress tackling a wildfire in the Cairngorms that broke out two weeks ago.

articles.title: Donald Trump says Andy Burnham told him he will ‘open up North Sea oil’
articles.raw_rss: The US president, who is a vocal supporter of fossil fuels, argues the move would make the UK ‘a wealthy country’.
articles.raw_meta: The US president, who is a vocal supporter of fossil fuels, argues the move would make the UK ‘a wealthy country’.
articles.jina_text:
Speaking in the White House, the US president said if the Prime Minister followed through on his commitment the UK was “going to be a wealthy country”.




Mr Trump also again warned that immigration is “killing” Britain, with “people coming from all over the world and just camping out”.








Following the phone call between the two leaders on Mr Burnham’s first day in office, Downing Street would not be drawn on any potential future plans for North Sea drilling after Mr Trump talked up a change in policy under Mr Burnham.




The US president, a vocal supporter of fossil fuels, has long championed the move as he has railed against “windmills”.




Mr Trump had lost a legal battle with the Scottish Government to stop a wind turbine development visible from his Aberdeenshire golf course.


Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke to Donald Trump on his first day in office (Kirsty Wigglesworth/PA)
PA Wire




Labour’s 2024 manifesto said the party would not issue new North Sea licences.




Ed Miliband, who held the energy and net zero brief under Sir Keir Starmer and had been a strong supporter of the election pledge, has now taken up the Foreign Secretary role.




His successor as Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, has said the manifesto was clear there is scope to exploit existing licences and that oil and gas are “part of the mix” going forward – but would not be drawn on whether there are plans to go further.


(PA Graphics)
PA Graphics




Referring to his conversation with Mr Burnham, Mr Trump said: “Well, he did say one very good thing.













“He said he’s going to open up North Sea oil.




“If he does that, you’re going to be a wealthy country.”




The president added: “They have two problems. They have a huge immigration problem – people coming from all over the world and just camping out in your country.




“He’s got that problem, and he’s got an energy problem.




“He’s got windmills all over the place, and any time you see windmills, you see a failing country.




“They’re made in China, not used by China, but they’re made in China.”


Donald Trump plays from the rough on a visit to his golf course near Aberdeen (PA)
PA Archive




He went on: “You have one of the most valuable oil finds anywhere in the world, and if the United Kingdom would use it, they’d be a wealthy country again. And I tell you what, I could not get Starmer to use it. It was incredible.”









Mr Trump said: “You have your own oil and gas. If you use the North Sea, the UK will be a really rich country. I cannot get the point across.




“The new gentleman, when I spoke to him, he said he’s going to open up the North Sea. Let’s see if that happens.”

Weatherwatch: rainclouds are travelling farther in warmer world


Climate crisis affects not only the amount of rain that falls but where, with implications for land use and water security




Have you ever wondered how far a raindrop has travelled before it lands on you? It may have journeyed thousands of kilometres from the ocean, sea or lake it evaporated from – and now research shows raindrops are travelling even farther than they used to.
Warmer air can hold more water vapour, and that is changing not only how much rain we receive but also where it falls. Travis Aerenson, of the University of Wyoming, and his colleagues modelled atmospheric moisture movements in the US over more than three decades. Their research showed that in the southwestern and southern plains, moisture in the atmosphere travels 30 to 50 miles (50 to 80km) farther than it did 35 years ago, staying aloft for an extra two to four hours before falling as rain.

Their findings, published in Geophysical Research Letters, also show that more evaporation is occurring from ocean surfaces and less from land surfaces. The change in atmospheric moisture pathways affects where and when precipitation occurs, with implications for land use. The researchers also note that the trend for moisture to travel farther will result in the water security of more countries and states falling increasingly outside their borders, requiring greater collaboration between neighbours.

articles.jina_text:
The Prime Minister is set to confirm the next tranche of funding for four new nuclear submarines to replace Britain's current beleaguered fleet. 
Andy Burnham will today set out £8.4billion in funding for the next phase of the Dreadnought nuclear submarine programme during a visit to Barrow-in-Furness in Cumbria.


The investment will advance construction of the new nuclear-armed submarines designed to succeed the ageing Vanguard-class fleet, which currently underpins the nation's continuous at-sea Trident deterrent.
Some £5.9billion of the spending announced today will go to BAE Systems, with the rest directed toward the wider supply chain.
Those figures form part of the £63billion ring-fenced for Britain's nuclear deterrence under the Defence Investment Plan.

Mr Burnham is expected to use the trip to promise that the spending will generate tens of thousands of jobs while strengthening hundreds of businesses across the country.
The Defence Nuclear Enterprise currently sustains around 47,000 jobs across Britain, a workforce projected to grow to 65,000 by the end of the decade, with 22,000 apprenticeships anticipated by 2035.

"To every young person across the country, I want you to know that there is a path for you into a reindustrialised Britain, and it starts with the apprenticeships we are funding through this investment today."

The investment will advance construction of the new nuclear-armed submarines to succeed the ageing Vanguard-class fleet | 
MINISTRY OF DEFENCE


HMS Dreadnought, the first of the quartet, is on track to finish sea trials and join the Royal Navy fleet in the early 2030s.
Under the new contract, the second vessel, HMS Valiant, will also advance to the sea trials stage, while the third and fourth boats will move forward through their respective construction phases.
The Dreadnought-class subs are built to be easier to sustain, with modern infrastructure and a trained workforce ready to support it when they arrive, according to the UK Defence Journal.

articles.jina_text:
Three Greek firefighters have died while tackling wildfires on the island of Crete and in the south of the mainland, the Greek fire department has said, as extreme heat hinders efforts to control blazes ravaging southern Europe.
The arc of brutal fires, which runs from the Atlantic coast to the eastern Mediterranean, and from the Scottish Highlands to the south of Spain, has alarmed experts because many of the fires have been out of control and burning close to towns and cities.

Temperatures exacerbated by the climate crisis reached 38C on Wednesday in Bordeaux in France, where firefighters kept a huge blaze in nearby pine forests from reaching the suburbs, and 37C in Madrid, west of which Spain’s largest wildfire on record had been “technically stabilised”, according to the interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska.
Dozens of ground crews had managed to contain the Madrid fire overnight, emergency services for the region said on Wednesday morning, but a separate fire near València, where temperatures will peak at a cooler 32C, is still out of control.


View image in fullscreen
Members of the Emergency Military Unit utilise controlled burns to halt the spread of wildfires in the Madrid border region in Cebreros, Ávila province, on Tuesday night. Photograph: Pablo Blázquez Domínguez/Getty Images
In televised comments from the Navalcarnero command centre on Wednesday morning, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said the situation near the capital was improving but stressed it was the first time in Spanish history that a wildfire had been raised to “operational level 3”, with the national government taking over the disaster response.
“I believe the next 12 hours will be very important,” he said. “They are going to be decisive in consolidating the work done by the national civil protection system.”


Accompanied by strong winds, the fourth heatwave of western Europe’s scorching summer has alarmed firefighters, who warn it makes blazes harder to quell and raises the risk of fires restarting in areas that have been stabilised. New fires also prompted evacuations in Greece and Turkey. 


View image in fullscreen
Wildfires in Crete, where authorities say two firefighters ‘fell heroically in the line of duty’. Photograph: ERT GR


View image in fullscreen
The remains of a firefighting vehicle seen south of Rethymno in Crete on Wednesday. Photograph: Costas Metaxakis/AFP/Getty Images
French authorities benefited from a calm night on Tuesday that allowed flare-ups to be swiftly extinguished but warned of “unfavourable” developing weather conditions that could hamper progress. The prefecture of Gironde said 126 firefighters had been injured since the start of the fire but the total burned area remained stable at 42,000 hectares (104,000 acres) on Wednesday morning.

articles.raw_content:
The French fire service has called it a ‘David vs Goliath’ battle – as 2,000 first responders fight to save industrial areas on the outskirts of Bordeaux.
Across France and Spain, more than 300,000 people have been forced to leave their homes. And it might still get worse. No rain is forecast until Friday – and that’s not expected to be heavy.
Meanwhile, another heatwave is on the way with temperatures set to rise to more than 40C in the affected regions.
Wildfires are becoming more frequent, more intense and lasting longer fuelled by climate change.
This year, Western Europe experienced the hottest June since records began – with rising temperatures straining ecosystems and infrastructure across the continent.
In this episode of the breakdown, we speak with Channel 4 News Correspondent Amelia Jenne, who is in France, and explore the damage being caused, and whether Europe can cope with wildfires becoming more intense with climate change driving ever more extreme temperatures.

articles.title: Half of England plunges into ‘flash drought’ after low rain and hot weather
articles.raw_rss: The Environment Agency has declared a drought across seven areas of southern, eastern and central England.
articles.raw_meta: The Environment Agency has declared a drought across seven areas of southern, eastern and central England.
articles.jina_text:
Swathes of England are suffering from “flash drought” as a result of very low rainfall and high temperatures, the Environment Agency has said.




The government agency said seven areas of central, eastern and southern England – around half of the country – have been declared as officially in drought.








The areas are East Anglia, Hertfordshire and the whole of London, Thames Valley, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, Devon and Cornwall, the West Midlands, and Wessex – covering Dorset, Somerset, Wiltshire and Gloucestershire.




With a few days left to go, this month could end up as the driest July on record, with England having just 7% of expected rainfall, and southern England seeing just 1%.




As a result, much of the country is experiencing a flash drought – one that has come on quickly despite a very wet winter, as a result of dry weather in the spring and summer and a series of heatwaves that put pressure on resources.




The announcement was made as parts of the UK experience their fourth heatwave of the summer, with temperatures reaching into the 30s in some places.


(PA Graphics)
PA Graphics




There were record-breaking heatwaves in May and June, and a third earlier this month, which have hit agriculture, rivers and the natural environment, prompted widespread wildfires and led to hosepipe bans for millions of people.













The Met Office announced that a new June temperature record of 38C has been confirmed, up from the 37.7C provisionally announced.




The UK and England record, set on June 26, came from the same station – Lingwood in Norfolk – as the provisional reading, the Met Office said.









Almost a third of England – including parts of the South East, Midlands and North West – is in “prolonged dry weather” status, with only the North East and Yorkshire still seeing “normal” conditions for the time of year.


(PA Graphics)
PA Graphics




It is the second year in a row with parts of the country suffering from drought, despite winter rainfall replenishing reservoirs and groundwater and helping the country through a dry spring without major impacts, the Environment Agency said.

articles.title: More than half of England officially in drought, Environment Agency says
articles.raw_rss: The drought declarations follow an exceptionally hot and dry period, which has hit rivers, crops and nature.
articles.raw_meta: The drought declarations follow an exceptionally hot and dry period, which has hit rivers, crops and nature.
articles.jina_text:
Drought has been declared across more than half of England as hot, dry weather takes its toll on the country's water supplies.
The Environment Agency (EA) has said that seven regions – covering large parts of central, eastern and southern England – are now in official drought conditions.
It added that the impacts are already being felt, including low river flows, early harvests and high risk of wildfires. More than 20 million people are already under hosepipe bans.
North Wales and the Upper Severn river basin entered drought conditions last week, Natural Resources Wales said.
Scotland does not declare drought but monitors "water scarcity". Some parts of eastern Scotland are in the most extreme category of "significant scarcity", according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency.







Hosepipe ban in force as drought threatens - is your area affected?





How climate change worsens heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and floods
"The hot and dry weather means we are currently using water faster than nature can replenish it," said Helen Wakeham, director of water at the Environment Agency and chair of the National Drought Group.
The full list of English regions in drought conditions are:

East Anglia
Hertfordshire and the whole of London
Thames Valley

the West Midlands 
Wessex, covering Dorset, Somerset, Wiltshire, and South Gloucestershire
There is no single definition of drought, but it usually refers to a period of prolonged unusually dry weather that can have impacts on people, nature and the environment. 
The EA considers all of these factors before deciding whether to declare a drought.
The declaration is a public sign that the EA is stepping up its response to the dry conditions, including increased monitoring and controls on how much water can be taken from rivers and groundwater. 
It can mean hosepipe bans being introduced if they are not already in place.


'Flash drought'

View image in fullscreen
Parched parkland at Greenwich in London, one of seven areas declared to be officially in drought by the Environment Agency. Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA


Half of England officially in ‘exceptionally serious’ drought


Environment Agency names seven regions affected by unusually hot and dry weather and shortage of water




Half of England is officially in drought, with July set to be the driest on record after winter floods, the Environment Agency has said.
The “flash drought” developed quickly because of unusually low rainfall and high temperatures.

The seven areas officially in drought are East Anglia, Hertfordshire and the whole of London, Thames Valley, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, Devon and Cornwall, the West Midlands, and Wessex (covering Dorset, Somerset, Wiltshire and south Gloucestershire).
Helen Wakeham, the director of water at the Environment Agency and chair of the National Drought Group, said: “The hot and dry weather means we are currently using water faster than nature can replenish it.


“A second consecutive summer drought is an exceptionally serious situation and one that will have long-lasting impacts on our environment, wildlife and the economy.
“We want everyone to stay safe and hydrated during the hot weather but every drop we can save is a drop more for nature and agriculture.”
Wednesday’s announcement means England has experienced drought in three of the past five years: 2022, 2025 and 2026.
July has had only 7% of the expected rainfall, falling to 1% across southern England, with no substantial rainfall on the way. Some parts of Devon have not experienced any rain for 50 consecutive days.
The Environment Agency said record winter rainfall had helped to replenish reservoirs and groundwater, but reservoir storage has now fallen to 7.4% below the average for this time of year.


View image in fullscreen
The Walthamstow Wetlands reservoirs in east London. England’s reservoir storage is below average for this time of year.  Photograph: Matthew Chattle/Future Publishing/Getty Images


Almost half of all reservoirs are classed as below normal levels, with Wimbleball, operated by South West Water, and Blagdon, operated by Bristol Water, both “exceptionally low”.
The Environment Agency said current water reserves “should be enough for the coming months until the next period of sustained rainfall”.
However, Will Lang, the Met Office’s chief meteorologist, said there was “little sign of the widespread, sustained rainfall that would be needed to make a significant difference to the areas most affected by the dry weather”.
In England, 40% of the population are under a hosepipe ban, with seven water companies – Affinity Water, Anglian Water, Cambridge Water, Southern Water, South East Water, Thames Water and South West Water – all restricting water use.

Thousands of emergency workers from across Europe have joined forces to battle wildfires around the French city of Bordeaux, and help with one of the largest evacuations the Continent has seen since the Second World War – even as new heatwaves threatens to worsen the raging blazes in France and Spain.



Sophie Brocas, prefect of Gironde and the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region, said the main fire, which has scorched 42,000 hectares – an area more than four times the size of Paris – had been “stabilised” as of Wednesday morning.



But alerts remained across the country with temperatures expected to reach 41°C.





Brocas said “mobilisation remains total” for relief operations. An estimated 2,500 firefighters, 1,500 military personnel and 1,200 police officers have been deployed around Bordeaux, according to local authorities.



Those fighting the blazes have been supported by a multinational mission under the European Union Civil Protection Mechanism, which has included firefighting planes and helicopters from the Czech Republic, Croatia, Germany, Portugal, Slovakia, Sweden and Turkey.

Jomain said the blaze was no longer growing but had not been extinguished. “

articles.raw_meta: Spain and France have so far borne the burnt of this summer's wildfires, caused by a succession of heatwaves and prolonged dry spells.
articles.jina_text:
Since mid-July wildfires have torn through France, Spain, and Portugal forcing more than 300,000 people to evacuate their homes.
Officials in the Spanish capital Madrid have said the fires are the worst the region have ever experienced.
French President Emmanuel Macron, visiting the fire-ravaged area in the Gironde region, called the "completely unprecedented" wildfire the "toughest since World War Two".


The fires have broken out amid a sweltering summer of heatwaves across Europe. Both France and Spain are now seeing another sharp rise in temperatures, with peaks of 41-42C expected in France.
Wildfires in the regions outside Madrid have burned about 606 sq miles (1570 sq km) since 1 July, according to the European Forest Fire Information System (Effis). That is an area more than twice as large as the city itself. 


















In France, the worst affected area has been the Gironde, around the city of Bordeaux, where more than 200,000 people were forced from their homes. 
From 22 July the blaze spread rapidly, tearing through forests and fields in France's famous wine region, and burning more than 162 sq miles (420 sq km) in less than four days - an area roughly four times the size of Paris.
At its peak, the wildfire came as close as nine miles (15km) from the south of Bordeaux, although the city was never under serious threat.
The fires have also came close to a number of sensitive military and industrial sites in the area, including facilities that work on French ballistic missiles, rocket motors, and the processing of hazardous chemicals.


The fires became so extreme they created their own giant fire thunderstorm. 
A rare weather event, storms like these are formed when heat from the wildfires makes the air above the fire rise rapidly, carrying smoke, ash and water vapour high into the atmosphere.
As the air rises, it cools, and the water vapour condenses into a cloud. If the fire is powerful enough and the atmosphere is unstable, that cloud can grow into a cumulonimbus - the same type of cloud associated with thunderstorms.










If these clouds then become large enough, they can produce their own lightning, which can then start new fires. They can also occasionally bring hail and rain.


These extreme and unpredictable conditions make the fires all the more difficult to stop.
To combat them, French firefighters have been using planes loaded with fire retardant, as well as planes like the Canadair, which can scoop 6,000 litres of water from lakes or the sea in 12 seconds and drop it directly on the fires.
On dangerous days, loaded aircraft patrol high-risk areas before any fires have been reported, so they can drop within minutes of a sighting. Planes often fly in a continuous shuttle while retardant is laid along the edges of the fire and ground crews attack the flames directly.
